column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article dates the move of the court to 1647; the entry says 'in the 1640s', which is consistent, so the year is left out to match the entry's wording. The article gives two accounts of the treasury (300,000 reals taken to Kediri, or 150,000 to Kediri and 200,000 left at Plered); only the lower bound 'at least 300,000' is given, attributed.

The article gives Raffles's governorship as 1813-1816 but says he sent the stone to India in 1812; the dates are left out because they contradict each other (and the entry says only 'the 19th century'). The article calls Airlangga 'one of the greatest kings in Javanese history'; not used.

The article writes the grandfather's name as 'Athan Che[ra]l Irumporai/Irumpurai'; the bracketed name is not printed and he is called a king of the Irumporai line. The article spells the village both Velayuthampalayam and Velayudhampalayam; both forms used as the article uses them. Climate figures, population and the paper mill's rankings left out. The entry's statement about Sangam poetry is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article's lead says the deed split New Jersey 'from 1674 until 1702', though the deed is dated 1 July 1676; the 1674 date is left out. The article spells Little Egg Harbor both 'Harbour' (in the quoted deed) and 'Harbor'; the entry uses 'Little Egg Harbor'.
The article's rankings (the only working gold mine in India, 40% of Karnataka's electricity, first in sweet lime) are left out. 'Chalukyas of Kalyani' is the article's 'Kalyani Chalukyas'.

The article spells the poet 'Sandhyakar Nandi' and gives his life as c. 1084-1155; the entry's spelling 'Sandhyakara Nandi' is used (checker may flag it). The entry calls the rebels Kaivartas in northern Bengal; the article's term 'Varendra rebellion' is used alongside.

The article's name form is 'Ramón de Bonifaz'; the entry's 'Ramón Bonifaz' is kept. The entry says he 'is regarded as the first admiral of Castile'; the article adds that some scholars consider the evidence weak, which is given as a hedge, not a contradiction. The entry dates the breaking of the bridge to May 1248; the article gives only 1248.

The article says the Thousand Days' War was 'accessory' to the chaos after the Coup of 1900; the entry dates it 1899-1902 and says Liberal opposition led to it. The coup of 1900 is left out to avoid a confused chronology. The article writes the National Bank 'in 1880', before the 1886 constitution; given as the article has it. Counts of electors (642 of 3,941) left out as unclear.
The article gives the Western Kingdom's ruler in the Chinese record as Wu-lao-po-wu, identified with Hayam Wuruk.
The article says both that he was one of the guards at Charles I's execution and that he 'claimed to have been present'; the entry states the former, and the point is not repeated here.
The entry dates the end of self-government to 1934; the article gives no year for the Commission of Government, so none is given here.

The entry has him as BSAC representative and administrator in North-Western Rhodesia from 1897 to 1907; the article gives representative from 1897 and commissioner from September 1900 to 1907, consistent. Left out the article's praise ('one of the most powerful', 'was praised').

The entry says Ross became an earldom in the early 13th century; the article says it was an earldom from the 12th century, the title being created several times from the mid-12th century. No date is given here for the earldom. The entry has John of Islay forfeiting the earldom in 1475; the article says it was vested in the crown in 1476. Left out. The article dates the capture of Dingwall castle by Donald to 1412, 'just before the battle of Harlaw', which the entry dates 1411. Left out.

The article gives 6,717 drawings in one place and 5,000 drawings by Mutis's pupils sent to Spain in another; the entry says more than 6,000. No drawing count is given here. The article says the joint publication was produced in 1937 and that 'in 1952 began the publication of the enormous work in its entirety'; the 1952 date is used for the full work.

The article says the scheme was proposed in August 1655 but its introduction was delayed to October; the entry dates the rule from August 1655. The October date is left out so the page does not seem to disagree with itself.

The article's ryotwari section is muddled (it first describes ryotwari as land revenue 'imposed on an individual or community owning an estate ... analogous to that of a landlord', then calls that assessment 'zamindari'); only the clearer statements are used.

The entry calls him maharaja from 1893; the article says he ruled from 1893 but was raised to hereditary Maharaja only in 1921 (Raja before). The text gives the 1921 elevation without calling him anything else from 1893, which may read as a tension with the entry's wording. The article says Lokendra Singh was 'derecognised' on 28 December 1971; given here in general terms.
The article spells the king Jayabhupati and Jayabupati; the entry's Jayabupati is used. The entry says four stones found 'near Cibadak in Sukabumi'; consistent.

The article says he returned to Burma in 1954 but also 'upon his return in 1953' founded the Tai Mining Company; the founding year is left out. The entry calls his wife Inge Sargent; the article gives Inge Eberhard (her maiden name). I used Eberhard for the marriage and did not print Sargent. The article says he sat in the Chamber of Nationalities from 1954; kept as given.

The article says Mariño retreated to Cumaná after the battle, then that Bolívar and Mariño arrived together in Caracas on 18 June; Mariño's movements are left out. Short article (about 340 words); the text stays close to the floor.

The article dates Catumandus's siege to 'just before ca. 390–387 BC'; given as shortly before about 390 BCE. Comanus's attack is placed at the Floralia in the article; left as 'a festival' to avoid a Roman festival name in a Greek setting without comment. Massalia, Nannus, Gyptis and Protis are named in the entry's own description, which the reader has just read.

The entry says he succeeded his father Sebetwane; the article says he succeeded his half-sister Mamochisane, who stepped down and proclaimed him. Neither predecessor is named in the text. The article says the Helmore party's survivors included Roger and Isabella Price, then that Isabella Price died; the survivors are left out. Birth year c. 1835 is from the article's heading dates; the entry gives only d. 1863.

28 February 1297 fell in the last month of 1296 by the Venetian calendar, as the article notes; the text keeps 1297, as the entry does. The Golden Book (1315) is already in the entry's description, so it is not repeated.

The article gives his governorship as 1532 to 1560, but also has him gilding temples in 1572, granting land in 1574 and 1579, handing power to Achyutappa about 1563 and dying in 1580. These later years are left out; the entry gives only the 16th century and around 1532. The entry spells the name Sevappa Nayak; the article uses Nayaka. The tax system described in the article (land tax, marriage tax, Jesuit accounts) is not clearly tied to Sevappa's own reign and is left out.

The entry says Rajaram appointed him Sachiv in 1697; the article says October 1690. The year is left out. The article spells the office Sacheev and Sacheeva and gives the surname as Gaudekar (title Gandekar); the entry's spelling Sachiv is used and the surname is not printed. The article calls the Mughal officer at Junnar Alibaig; left unnamed.

The entry says he fled to Ava; the article says he fled to Möng Yang and was captured there by an Ava expedition at Möng Kawng. Where he fled is left out; the capture by Ava is kept. The entry's spelling Mong Mao is used; the article writes Möng Mao (the checker may flag it). Other places keep the article's spelling (Möng Yang, Möng Ting). The article gives his reign as 1413 to 1442 and his death as 1446; the entry gives only the 15th century. The accounts of his death differ, and all three are attributed.

The entry calls him deputy commissioner of the Bechuanaland Protectorate; the article calls him resident commissioner. Neither title is printed for the protectorate. The article says he discussed the plan with Rhodes 'while at Oxford in 1878', which does not fit his degree of 1863; the year is left out. The article says he 'governed with conspicuous success' (from an old source); not repeated.

The article's account of the garrison commander is confused (Soleyman/Suleiman Aqa executes his commander and places a nephew in charge; later Soleyman Aqa is said to recapture the city after being sent to Shiraz). Only the surrender and the dispatch to Shiraz are kept. The Basrans' claim to have killed 2,000 besiegers for 2 wounded is left out as a one-sided figure. Omani entry into Basra: 'mid-October and on the 14th'; given as October 1775.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; it adds only the owners' names, plantation counts and the company's late closure, and its dates (sales to 1818, offices closed 1821) go past the entry's end date of 1795 The article says the owners acquired the colony from the French on 24 October 1714 (the entry: ransomed from a French raid in 1712), and that the company kept operating after the British cession until it sold its last plantations in November 1818 and closed its offices in 1821; the entry's dates are 1720–1795.

The article calls Solomon Mahlangu 'an exile of the 1976 Soweto uprising'; the entry says he was hanged in 1979. Not repeated. Former teachers listed in the article (Ruth First, Jack Simons, etc.) are left out.

The article's statement that their ancestors arrived around 200–500 AD and descend from the Khoi conflicts with its own figure of Khoe-San ancestry above 20%; both left out. The article argues for Barolong seniority in a one-sided passage ('By right the Barolong are Senior'); only the fact of the dispute is kept. The article says 'various African groups' founded the Transvaal and Orange Free State; worded neutrally. The entry names the Pedi of north-eastern South Africa; the article's Northern Sotho include the Bapedi.

The confirmed article is the Soulbury Commission, whose work produced the constitution; the text keeps to the commission's recommendations and the constitution's adoption. The quotation 'any attempt by artificial means...' is paraphrased in reported speech; the article gives it as the commissioners' words.

The article says the Article 47 prison term rose 'from three to five years' and elsewhere 'from a maximum of six months to a maximum of five years'; only the new maximum is given. The old fine (50,000 francs) is also left out with it. The article's claim that an Article 47(b) protected Jewish clients' assets from Nazi Germany is unsourced and doubtful; left out. Its 'Rubik Agreements' of 3 March 2015 also left out (date doubtful). Rankings ('most strict in the world') left out. The entry says the secrecy was greatly reduced from 2009; the article argues the revisions had little effect. The text reports the measures without either judgement. The article's chronology of the drafting (late 1920s, then 'as the first World War commenced') is confused; left out.

The article says the Casa das Minas 'must have been founded' in the 1840s; hedged as probably. The entry gives the nineteenth century. Heading 'How it was used' is for practice; the religion is living and is told in the present tense where it describes belief.

The article says Mutallu of Kummuh, an Assyrian vassal, was placed on the Kammanean throne in Tarhunazi's place; the entry says Melid became an Assyrian province and part of its territory went to Kummuh. Mutallu's role is left out. The entry calls him the last king of Melid; not repeated, given the article's account of a successor. The article gives his reign as c. 719–712 BCE; the entry gives fl. 712 BCE.

The excavators' periodisation puts the fire between Phase 3 (c. 3450–3350 BC) and Phase 4 (c. 3350–3200 BC); given as around 3350 BCE. The article names Warsaw University's Polish Center of Archaeology; shortened to the University of Warsaw. Golden statuettes dated Naqada IIIB (c. 3200–3000 BC) or possibly IIIA; date left out.
SKIPPED: the article's account of the schools (about 200 words) is already told in full in the entry's description; the rest is about family upbringing in Tenochtitlan, not the telpochcalli

The article traces the Renati Chodas to Nandivarman around 500 CE and dates the Kalamalla Telugu inscription of the Renati king Erikal Mutturaju Dhanunjaya to 575 CE, and says the Konidena Chodas ruled from 950. These dates fall before the entry's 11th–14th century and are left out. The entry's Manumasiddhi, patron of Tikkana, appears in the article's list as Manumasiddharasa; Tikkana is not named in the article. The article says five Velanati chieftains ruled, but lists six; no number is given.
SKIPPED: article under 400 words, nearly all of it already in the entry's description (burials, skulls, isotopes, DNA); too little left for a longer text
The entry spells the name Teraupoʻo; the article writes Teraupo'o. The entry's dates are fl. 1880s–1897; the article gives c. 1855 – 23 December 1918, used here as they do not contradict the entry.

The article says the captives were marched 2,000 miles to Veracruz in the lead and from Santa Fe to Mexico City later; the text avoids the route and keeps the entry's wording intact (held until 1842).
The entry's fossa regia, Byzacena and mosaics are not in the article; nothing added on them. The article lists Securo as Donatist and the 646 council as antimonotelite.

The article calls Hubert his 'eldest brother' but lists Theobald first among the children; birth order left out. John Lodge's 1789 marriage year (1189), which the article says no other author follows, left out.
The article gives his birth as c. 1790; the entry says 1790. Article is short (about 270 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The article gives the execution as November 1768 in its lead and 4 December 1768 in the section on his execution; the text says only 'late in 1768'. The Chinese source makes him Ekkathat's elder half-brother, the Thai chronicles the third prince; birth order left out.

The article says the craft dates back to the Rajput era and also that Nathu ji Soni invented the process in 1767; both kept, as the entry gives no date. The entry's green, red or blue glass is not in the article. The entry says 'a few families'; the article says the secret stays in one family; the text does not say how many families practise it. The article's two accounts of the process (terracotta paste; lac-resin board) are given as two descriptions.
The article dates the strategy to 'the early 1980s'; the entry says from 1979. The text gives no start year for the programme itself.
The article is short (about 270 words); the text uses nearly all of it beyond what the entry already says.

The entry calls him the first governor; the article says first Lieutenant-Governor. The text names no title. The article spells his father 'Christoper' (probably Christopher); his name left out. The entry's choice of Fredericton as capital is not in the article.

The entry spells the poems Selalihini Sandeshaya and Kavyasekharaya; the article writes Salalihini Sandeshaya and Kawyashekaraya. The article also names the king Parakkramabahu VI. Left out: the claim that some historians and critics hold the incorrupt body in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa to be his, and that it will stay intact until 4230; the folklore of exorcism. The article spells the cave both Indurigiri and Indurugiri.

The entry calls Toera the last king of Menabe; the article calls him 'a king' and names his great-grandson Georges Harea Kamamy as a present Sakalava king. The text does not call him the last. The article spells the half-brother both Ingraza and Ingereza.
The article says that 'since 1445' Masachika had faced resistance from the warriors of Kaga, which does not fit the entry's birth year of 1455; the year is left out.

The entry names Granada and Aragon as the threats; the article names the Order of Santiago and Granada. Only Granada is named ('among others'). The article dates the signing 'around April 2, 1243' and 'April 1243'.
The entry names the parties as the Seneca and Robert Morris; the article's lead calls it a treaty between the Seneca Nation and the United States. The text names neither as the formal party.

The entry says the assembly was dominated by the Liberals; the article says half its 80 members were to be chosen by each side. The text gives the number of members only and leaves out how they were chosen.
The article says the treaty is dated 13 February 1874 but that some place it around March; the text gives the treaty's own date and the doubt. The entry gives only 1874.
The article lists the Słupsk meeting as 1287 in one place and as November 1284 in another; no year is given for it here.

The entry names the Lord of the Isles John MacDonald II; the article calls him John of Islay, Earl of Ross, which is used here. The article's lead says the lands north of the Firth of Forth were to be divided between the Lord of the Isles and the Earl of Douglas, while the entry gives the north to the Lord of the Isles and his kinsmen; the division is not restated here.

The article's lead says Colbert created the Compagnies Franches de la Marine in 1674, while its Organization section has them created by the ordinance of 16 December 1690; the text does not call the 1690 companies the first. The article says the troops were sent to New France in 1682 and were the only regulars there from 1682; the entry gives 1683, so 1682 is left out.

The article dates the Buraimi action both 25 and 26 October 1955; only the month is given here. The article says the name change was decided in late 1955 and also that the force was renamed in 1956; the renaming year is left to the entry. The school section dates its opening to May 1961 but then speaks of 1954; the school is left out.
The article's account of the Passavas massacre is ambiguous about who was slaughtered; the text keeps its wording without naming the victims.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, most of it already in the description; it says nothing of Toggenburg
The article gives his birth both as c. 1806 and as 1806; the text says around 1806. The article spells the Yauri emir both Yakuba and Yakubu; Yakuba is used.
The article spells Kurd I and Kurd II also as Kurt; Kurd is used.
The article says all princely states were merged into Rajasthan before 1947; the entry says Dungarpur and Banswara lasted as princely states until 1948. The merger is left out.

The article says Divya, Rudok and Bhima ruled Varendra for around half a century and that Bhima alone ruled for 30 years; the entry says the rebels held Varendra for a generation. No length of rule is given here.
The article gives an administration 'as of September 2026' without names; council membership is not listed here.

The entry spells the name Warpalawa; the article has Warpalawas II, Warpallawas and Urpallâ. The article names his son Muwaḫḫaranis II as his successor; the entry says Tuwana fades from the record after his reign, so the succession is left out. The article dates his reign c. 740 to c. 705 BCE.
The transport-rider story comes from Jose Burman, quoted at length in the article; it is told here as one account.

The article dates his deposition some time between c. 739 and c. 732 BCE; the entry says around 730 BCE, so no year is given. The article says Assyrian sources call his successor Ḫullî a son of a nobody, usually denoting a commoner, but that he may have been the nephew of the vassal king Ruwas; the entry calls him a commoner, so his identity is left out.

The article says Wube withdrew inland in 1844 and finally left Tigray in 1846; the entry says he ruled Tigray from 1831 to 1855. The end of his rule in Tigray is left out. The article mentions sources that have him die in 1855 but says 1867 is more commonly accepted; the text gives 1867, as the article's lead does.
The article dates the move to Chouchi to c. January 297; the entry gives 296, so no date is given for it here.

The article gives his birth as c. 1263 and death c. 1312/13; consistent with the entry's d. c. 1312. The 1329 inscription's claim that he reigned as Athinkhaya II is reported as an alternative to the chronicles, as the article does.
The entry speaks of Morisco refugees; the article does not mention them, so they are not repeated here. Left out the garbled sentence about a war with the Maltese.
Distance: the entry says about 40 km south of Udaipur, the article about 35 km from Udaipur. Neither figure is printed here.
SKIPPED: the article's account of his life is already given in full by the entry; the rest is a list of family members
SKIPPED: article too thin: a short definition (whose dates, 1979 and 1999, differ from the entry's 1904-1979), a paragraph on identity and a list of notable people

The article spells the kingdom both Limmu-Ennarea and Limmu Ennerea; the entry's spelling is used. His marriage to Genne Minjoti in 1823 predates the 1825 coup; reported under Reign only as a fact of his marriages.
The entry says Makau died at Zuba; the article says he was killed in battle at the gates of Lapai. The place of his death is not printed here.
The entry dates the end to 1856, when Walker revoked the charter; the article dates Walker's seizure of power and of the company's assets to 1855. No year is given here for the seizure.
The entry dates the crushing Maratha and Awadh defeat to 1751; the article gives no year for the defeats, only his return in 1752 after promising half his lands. The defeat is left undated here.
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 300 words of text, nearly all of it already in the entry's description
Left out the claim about a great-grandson, Baba Suwari of Wenchi, which sits oddly with the disputed 13th- or 15th-century dating.

Birth: the entry gives c. 1922; the article says around 1919, perhaps earlier (95 at death), though it also says he was 22 on taking the throne in 1944. No birth year or age is printed here. Death: the article gives both 24 and 25 April 2011; only April 2011 is printed. The entry says he remained a central figure in Afar regional politics after 1991; the article says disputes led to his marginalisation from the new Afar Region's politics. Neither is printed. The entry says exile in Saudi Arabia and an Afar Liberation Front led by his family; the article says only that he fled the country and established the ALF. The ALF's founding is left out.

The article also says English invasions of the 12th and 13th centuries disrupted Ó Fearghail rule and claims a Nugent-Delvin 'Honour' covering 30% of Longford from a 1172 de Lacy grant; these sit against the entry's statement that the O'Farrells kept Annaly largely free of the Anglo-Norman lords of Meath, and the Nugent section reads as advocacy. Both are left out. The entry spells the family Uí Fergail / O'Farrells; the article Ó Fearghail.
The Mino are named without a gloss: the source names them only in its schedule.

The entry calls Ariconium a Romano-British town; the article says some archaeologists see dispersed centres of settlement rather than a Roman town. That view is left out here, and the text does not call it a town either.

The article gives Arikesari's reign as c. 930-955 but his sons' reigns from c. 941; the dates are left out here. The entry names the Adipurana as also written at his court; the article mentions only the Vikramarjuna Vijaya, so the Adipurana is not repeated.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 210 words could be written beyond the entry, on Vajrayudha's accession in 770 and the brothers' rivalry

The article's lead gives his death as 1564 at Tunja, while its body says he died in Bogotá in 1552 (the entry's year). Neither the year nor the place of death is printed here. The entry names the battle of Bonza; the article says the two-week struggle culminated in a battle near Paipa, which it confusingly also calls the Battle of Vargas Swamp. Neither name is given to the 1539 fight here.

The article says he succeeded his father in 1738; the entry's dates give his reign as 1740-1770. The accession year is left out. The article names the father Raja Mansaram Singh; the entry's spelling Mansa Ram is used. The article is thinly sourced and partisan in tone (e.g. Shah Alam 'back stabbed him'); its wording on the Treaty of Benares is unclear and is followed closely.
The article dates the Siete Leyes to 1834; the entry says 1836. The year is left out.

The article puts the Regulators at about 2,200; the entry says about 2,000. The figure is left out. The article says the Regulators had a command structure and most had militia training; the entry calls them poorly led. That point is left out.

The entry says Moshoeshoe's letter allowed Cathcart to withdraw; the article says the British had already left Berea before the letter was sent and received it at their Caledon camp. The text says only that it reached him at the camp. The article's prelude dates are muddled (a Platberg meeting on 13 November and cattle collected by 18 November, then the march on 20 December); those November dates are left out. The entry spells Basotho; the article Basuto.

The entry spells the victor Amari Ngone Sobel Fall; the article has Amary Ngoné. The entry's spelling is used. The entry dates the battle c. 1549; the article gives 1549. No year is given in the text.

The article says the engagement at Fangtou was a stalemate and the decisive defeat came at Xiangyi during the retreat; the entry says Murong Chui defeated Huan Wen near Fangtou. The text tells the retreat from Fangtou and the ambush at Xiangyi without saying where the battle proper was.

The article calls Gawakuke the final battle between Gobir and Sokoto; the entry says raids and border wars continued for decades. The 'final battle' claim is left out. The entry spells Muhammad Bello; the article Muhammed Bello. The entry's spelling is used. The entry names the coalition as Gobir and Katsina-Maradi; the article names Gobir, the Tuareg and Maradi.
The entry lists Kildare's allies as from the Pale, Ulster and Connacht; the article says Leinster, Ulster and Connacht. Both are compatible.

The entry places the battle near Suphan Buri; the article says the location is disputed between Suphanburi and Kanchanaburi provinces (the Fine Arts Department in 1988 found little evidence for the Suphanburi stupa). The text mentions only that the stupa identification was questioned, not the dispute over the battle site. The article gives the chronicle date as 25 January 1593 and the recalculated date as 18 January; Burmese accounts put the battle in February 1593. The entry's 'early 1593' is kept by not naming a day.
The entry spells Pulakeshin; the article Pulakesin. The entry's spelling is used. The article is short and loosely written; its claims about the outcome are attributed to historians as it gives them.
The article gives the number of prisoners variously as 180, 183, almost 200 and 200 (on Kawau); the entry says about 180. No number is given in the text.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, and much of it is already in the description

The article gives his reign as 1777-1795 and his life as c. 1715 - c. 1790 (and the Katsina defeat around 1790); the entry dates his reign 1771-1789. No reign or death year is given in the text. The article says 'Bawa is also remembered for establishing Alkalawa as a new capital' in a paragraph about his father; it is unclear which ruler is meant, so it is left out.

The article contradicts itself on Keonjhar: it says Adi Bhanja's brother Jyoti Bhanja founded Keonjhar (implying the 8th century) and that Jyoti Bhanj was enthroned in the 12th century. No date is given for Keonjhar's founding. The article's claims that the dynasty originated before the Gupta Empire and that the Kanika branch dates from around the third century are left out as doubtful.

The article dates the first Maratha invasion of Bengal under him to 1741 and the invasion of the Haihaiyavanshi kingdom to the close of 1740; the entry says he conquered Ratanpur in 1741 and led the raids into Bengal from 1742. Neither year is given for those events. The entry says he was killed at a meeting held to negotiate peace; the article calls it an entertainment. The text follows the article without contradicting the entry.
The article gives the area as 10.7 hectares; the entry says about 10 hectares. The total is not repeated.
The entry says about 1,500 Black Loyalists founded the settlement; the article gives no number.

The article says that in later times men of non-Ahom families, such as those of Garhgayan Patar and Maran Patar, were also made Borpatragohain; the entry says the office was reserved for particular Ahom noble clans. Left out. The article's passage on the Chutia Borpatra official being retained until late in Suklenmung's reign and killed after a Brahmin's rebellion is unclear about who was killed; left out. Entry spelling Borpatrogohain used throughout; the article mostly writes Borpatragohain.
The entry places Buddu on the western shore of Lake Victoria; the article says the north-west shore. The shore is not named in the text.
The article gives the enlarged battalion as about 450 men and, a few paragraphs later, as about 400; the text says several hundred.
The entry spells the queen Camadevi; the article mostly writes Jamadevi in its narrative sections. The entry's spelling is used.

The article says the terms Canada East and Canada West were used 'from 1841 to 1843', which sits oddly with the entry's 1841-1867; the text does not give an end year for them. The article's figure of about $200 for the Grand Trunk Railway's annual income is plainly a slip; left out.

The entry dates the cycle to the 9th-10th century. The article reports Jenny Rowland's view that the two poems to Gwên belong to the earliest stratum, of the late eighth to the mid-ninth century, while some poems to the other sons are very late, perhaps the twelfth century. The figures are left out; the text says only that the Gwên poems are among the earliest.
The saved article is about the siege of 1580; its background section describes the castle itself, so the text covers both.

The article calls the 1938 Allahabad meeting the first All India Music Conference; 'first' is left out as doubtful. The article's list of 'dancers and musicians' at his court names writers such as Makhan Lal Chaturvedi and Mahaveer Prasad Dwivedi; left out. The dancer the article names as Karthik Kalyan (1939) and Kalyan Das (1943) is left unnamed.
The article dates l'Olive's appointment as captain general to 2 December 1837, clearly a slip for 1637; left out. Entry spelling l'Olive used; the article writes L'Olive.
The article dates the Palatine Law to 1454 but also says the ministries existed in Ayutthaya 'before 1455'; the text says 'before King Trailokanat's reform'.

The entry says the descendants form a distinct people in Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe; the article says most former chikunda merged into their host communities and only a few remote communities keep the identity. The text says only that the identity survives in communities around the Zambezi-Luangwa confluence. The article puts the chikunda 'at their height in the 17th century', when one prazeiro could have 5,000 or more, but also says the term was not in general use then; the figures for that period are left out.

The entry says the committee was led by Lorrin A. Thurston; the article names Henry E. Cooper as its chairman, chosen at a mass meeting on 14 January 1893. The text names no leader of the committee. The article dates the landing of marines to the afternoon of 16 January although it puts the start of the revolution on 17 January; the text gives no day for the landing.

The article calls the 1890 meeting a Constitutional Conference; the entry calls it the Federation Conference. It is called a conference in Melbourne here.

The article says the government devalued the bolívar 'by 100%', which is unclear; left out. 'Declared bankruptcy to the international banking community' rendered as declaring it could not pay.
